📢⚡Tell Congress to Stop Funding Bitcoin and Driving Up Our Electric Bills

The next time our PECO or PPL bill shows up higher than expected, remember this: a big chunk of the extra cost comes from cryptocurrency mining and the broader energy surge it drives.

In a conversation I had with former U.S. Bankruptcy Judge David R. [NAME] — who oversaw several major cryptocurrency bankruptcy cases, including Core Scientific (one of the largest crypto miners) — we both agreed: crypto functions, in practice, not as a currency but as a commodity whose worth is fundamentally based on the cost of the electricity needed to produce it. Judge [NAME] saw this reality up close while managing the financial wreckage of collapsed mining and crypto lending operations.

₿ Bitcoin isn’t “digital gold.” It is a commodity whose value is directly tied to the massive amounts of electricity required to mine it. Miners only make money if they can sell their Bitcoin for more than it costs to produce — and electricity is by far the biggest cost. As more bitcoins are mined, the network becomes harder to solve, so each new Bitcoin requires more electricity than earlier ones. [NAME] investors understood this dynamic: they were betting that Bitcoin’s price would keep rising as the power needed to mine the next coin grows higher. The more expensive it becomes to produce, the higher the price must go for miners to stay profitable. That’s why Bitcoin now trades in roughly the same range as the current cost to mine it — around $80,000.

Cryptocurrency mining now consumes between 0.6% and 2.3% of all electricity in the United States — roughly the same amount used by entire states like Washington or West Virginia. Because electricity demand is relatively inelastic in the short term, this added load has helped push our power bills up by 5–10% in many PJM areas through higher base rates and capacity charges. 

Here in PA-6, where families already stretch paychecks amid high housing costs and inflation, electricity prices are climbing. Recent rate increases, driven in part by surging demand from cryptocurrency mining operations across PJM, are hitting households hard. Utilities are upgrading infrastructure and securing more capacity, and guess who pays? Not just the miners or tech giants — we do, through higher base rates that don’t care whether we own crypto or not. In other words, when we look at our next PECO or PPL bill, 5–10% of it could be going to support cryptocurrency mining.

Beyond higher bills, the environmental toll is severe. Crypto mining’s explosive electricity demand is keeping older coal-fired plants running longer and increasing carbon emissions across the PJM region, where new load is often met by coal and natural gas. In PJM, this creates “carbon leakage”: demand from crypto operations pulls more coal-generated power from Pennsylvania, Ohio, and West Virginia, raising local emissions and worsening air quality for Chester and Berks County families.

Right here in Pennsylvania, operations like the Scrubgrass and Panther Creek waste-coal plants have ramped up burning specifically to feed crypto mining, spiking sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and CO₂ output. Globally, Bitcoin mining alone has been equivalent to burning tens of billions of pounds of coal in emissions impact. This isn’t clean innovation — it’s dirty externalities that all Pennsylvanians breathe and pay for.

The late Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett’s longtime partner and one of the clearest thinkers in American business, cut through the hype years ago. He called Bitcoin “stupid,” “evil,” and something that makes its promoters look bad in comparison to honest work. Munger warned that it undermines sound money and creates massive externalities. He was right. We’re all subsidizing a speculative asset that delivers no goods, no services, and no productivity — just higher bills and dirtier air for the rest of us.

Blockchain technology has legitimate uses: secure supply chains, fraud-resistant records, efficient contracting in specific industries. Those applications deserve support. But proof-of-work crypto mining — the dominant model for Bitcoin — is different. It turns kilowatt-hours into lottery tickets, and Pennsylvania ratepayers and taxpayers are footing part of the tab while the grid strains and emissions rise.

Now comes the latest proposal in Washington: the BITCOIN Act, introduced by Senator Cynthia Lummis and Representative [NAME]. This legislation directs the Treasury to purchase 1 million Bitcoins over the next five years — 200,000 BTC per year — and hold them for at least 20 years. At current prices, that’s a government commitment of roughly $80 billion in new purchases on top of the hundreds of thousands of BTC already held from forfeitures.

The bill claims this spending is “budget-neutral,” but the mechanism is clear: it diverts the first $6 billion per year in Federal Reserve remittances — money that currently helps reduce the federal deficit or fund general government operations — straight into buying Bitcoin. In plain terms, Washington wants to redirect tens of billions of taxpayer-backed dollars to stockpile a volatile digital commodity whose rising price is fueled by the very electricity demand driving up our utility costs here in Pennsylvania.
